idiom_name: state struct owned by one module + stateless render functions taking `const struct app_state *`
implementation_notes: C has no component tree to hook into, so the split is hand-written: one translation unit owns a `struct app_state` together with the functions that mutate it, and every renderer is a pure function of a `const struct app_state *` that only formats or draws. Events arrive as function pointers (stored in the state owner or passed in), which mutate the state and ask the caller to redraw - the immediate-mode discipline used by terminal and immediate-mode GUI toolkits. The classic structure is replaced by convention: the owner never renders, the renderers never mutate. Hand-writing it is still justified when the same renderers must serve a test harness that supplies a literal state struct, and when embedding a template engine would cost more than the markup it produces.
pitfalls: A renderer that writes to the state struct or to a global silently becomes a second owner; take `const` pointers and let the compiler enforce the direction of the dependency.
Format strings assembled from user data are an injection hole - route every value through one dedicated escape helper instead of sprinkling quotes into fprintf calls.
Event callbacks that do not receive an owner pointer (`void *user`) force the state back into globals, which is exactly the coupling the split removes.
